The booking confirmation lists the check-in code as 4827. I copied the message into these notes so I would not need to search my inbox at the door.

The rest of the message described the flat. There is a small table by the window, enough room for a laptop and a notebook, and a reading lamp next to the armchair. The kitchen faces the courtyard. The host asked guests to close the courtyard gate gently because the latch is loose. None of that changes how we enter the building, but I kept the details with the booking information.

I also wrote down what to carry in the small bag: a charger, the paperback I am halfway through, and a spare shirt. The larger bag can stay in the luggage rack until we reach the station. I would rather avoid opening both bags on the platform. The train ticket is saved on my phone, and I printed a copy because the screen is difficult to read outside.

The arrival plan is deliberately simple. We will walk from the station to the building and leave the bags before looking for somewhere to eat. I have not chosen a restaurant. There is no need to fit another reservation around the train, and we can decide once we know whether we are hungry. If the weather is unpleasant, we can eat whatever we brought for the journey and go out later.

Before leaving home, I need to close the windows, take out the rubbish and move the plant away from the radiator. Those are reminders for me, not instructions from the host. I put them in a separate paragraph so I would not confuse the things to do before departure with the information needed on arrival. The host's message remains the source for entering the flat; my packing list and departure reminders do not add any access information.
